endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Plan alternative workflow(s) for downtime and potential sunsetting

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Notification timelines for outages and dependency failures: Including outages of upstream providers (e.g., the cloud or foundation model vendor) not owned directly by the AI vendor.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Document GAI risks associated with system value chain to identify over-reliance on third-party data and to identify fallbacks.

endorsements.title: Drone-delivered automated external defibrillators in prehospital emergency care: implementation evidence, bottlenecks, and conceptual integration with artificial intelligence and next-generation communications
endorsements.quote: If AI analysis is unavailable or uncertain, conventional dispatcher protocols should remain the default.

commentary.bottom_line: Four sources, three of them frameworks from CHAI and NIST, recommend that health systems keep backup workflows for times when AI tools are down or reject requests, but no supplied study tests whether such workflows prevent care disruption. No supplied study documents the size of the hazard either, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests backup workflows, and no study measures how often or how badly care processes fail during AI downtime. The four endorsements are frameworks and one commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks for alternative workflows for downtime and sunsetting, and NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to document third-party dependencies and identify fallbacks. Both use should language and are voluntary. The supplied sources do not cite any federal or state rule that requires AI downtime procedures.

The CHAI playbook extends outage planning to upstream cloud and foundation model vendors that the AI vendor does not control. This suggests that contracts may need notification timelines covering those parties. The supplied sources give no data on the staffing or cost of keeping manual fallback workflows current and rehearsed.

commentary.research_gap: No supplied study measures how often AI outages or request rejections disrupt care, or compares sites with and without defined backup workflows on delays, errors, or missed tasks during downtime. Simulation or downtime-drill studies and analyses of real outage events could supply the first direct evidence, including whether staff retain manual skills after long periods of AI use.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net sites with thin staffing, and services such as AI-supported interpretation or patient messaging, may depend more heavily on AI tools, but the supplied evidence cannot confirm or size that risk.
